Turtle Rescue

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Every year dozens of baby turtles wash out on the beaches of the cape. If not rescued they will die. Carte Blanche investigates.

Unique Selling Point:
From March till September is a busy time for the Two Oceans Aquarium when sea turtles are being brought in to their rehabilitation centre. These tiny sea creatures are found frozen on the beaches of the Cape coast lifeless and still. They are cold and starving, suffering from dehydration and hypothermia and in a permanent state of shock. Referred to as ‘cold stunning’ their heart rate have decreased to a point that they will die if not rescued.

Summary:
Turtles are cold blooded and cannot warm themselves. They thrive in the warm waters of KwaZulu-Natal and Mozambique where they breed during the summer months. They lay their eggs onshore in the the sand and after 60 days these tiny animals fight their way into the sea heading into the warm current where they drift and float whilst feeding. But some get lost in stormy seas and cross currents drifting kilometres south into the icy waters of the cape. From Plettenberg Bay on the east coast to Witsand on the west coast it is believed that hundreds of turtles wash ashore every year but only a few are the lucky ones found by passers by and picked up.

Human intervention is needed to rescue the stranded animals; some with injuries and damaged flippers they are in urgent need of medical attention. But it is not only the babies that need rescuing; adult turtles are often found by fisherman or divers out in the open seas where they are entangled in fishing lines. Plastic bags that float in the ocean looks like jellyfish, a staple diet of loggerhead turtles who are often found with plastic in their gut. Even baby turtles poop minute plastic pellets called nurdles that have become one of the biggest polluters of our oceans.

From Loggerheads to Leatherbacks, all seven species of turtles found in South Africa has been treated by a team of experts at the Two Oceans rehabilitation centre since its inception in 2009. They have seen the damage first hand that man causes: from treating infected and gashed carapice caused by boat propellers to removing plastic bags from the gut of a Loggerhead, they have managed to turn the statistics around.


Further information:
Talitha Noble, a 28 year old marine biologist working at the Two Oceans Aquarium has developed a special bond with turtles. Her daily job consist of feeding them a special diet, monitoring their growth, exercising the ones with damaged flippers and getting them ready to be released back into the ocean when they are strong enough. She says “they are my babies and have given me life lessons that no other school could have done. They come in here in all shapes and forms, some hardly breathing and when they leave, I have say goodbye to some very special ones like Sandy.

Sandy, a Green Turtle, was found near Witsand 2016 with big gashes through her carapace. It was suspected that she was hit by a boat propeller: we cleaned her wounds, removed the sand and debris under her damaged carapace; disinfected her and constantly monitored her progress and two years later we were able to release her. The amazing thing about science is that we are able to track her movements from the satellite tagging system we installed on the top of her carapice. Sandy has spent most of her time moving between Elands Bay and Lambert’s bay. She has now covered 1 223km, at an average pace of about 16 km per day.

Kevin Spiby, is the expert on fitting the satellite tracking system onto the adult turtles and making sure the batteries are in place and the system is working 100% before the release. He has been part of the team since inception and has got the fitting of the satellite system to the carapace down to a tee. Monitoring the movements of the turtles is the job of Maryke Mosson, the curator of the aquarium. She tracks their location and where they are heading for; how many kilometres they swim a day and how long they are stationed in each part of the ocean. This valuable data provides a reliable source of information on each of the adult turtles they have released back into the wild.

Twenty-six year old Inge Adams got hooked onto wildlife when she was a kid watching National Geographic programmes at her grandmother’s house. Today she is the youngest of the team with a master’s degree in marine biology. “I have found that my biggest strength comes from the fact that I see women as powerful and role models - gone are the days that a science team consisted of males only. Our sea turtles have been ambassadors for us and through their resilience and feistiness we learn life lessons ourselves and have given many children who have never laid their eyes on these creatures the chance to see them up close and learn about them.

“My day to day job is to gather data which becomes part of the studies of the turtle which I hope will give us a new insight into their behavioural patterns.” One of my favourites was Noci, a male loggerhead found near Witsand In April 2018 with major external injuries. He had barnacles on his carapace which indicated that he had been floating for some time. Our vet treated him with antifungal creams, vitamins, antibiotics and together we nursed him back to life. Noci and Sandy have both been back in the ocean for 78 days, and Noci, has racked up the fastest average speed of all our tagged turtles. He has covered a very impressive 4122 km since release in December, with an average pace of 53 km per day.

In December last year 14 juveniles were released together with Moya, a green turtle found near Sedgefield in October 2017 that had large open wounds on his flipper and totally dehydrated.
Pemba, an olive ridley turtle has travelled 14 388 km over the last year and is currently 1 917 km west of Africa. Just another 3 500 km to go and she will be off the coast of Brazil, where many Olive Ridley turtles breed.

Yoshi covered more than 18 500 km averaging 39.4 km per day. Since her release Yoshi has crossed various borders, against the currents and right now it appears as if Yoshi is swimming towards Australia where Loggerhead turtles nest.
Why are they amazing? Sea turtles have their own internal compass and can therefor adjust the direction in which they swim. They are able to sense the earth's magnetic field. Deep inside their brains, tiny crystals of a mineral called magnetite - which is magnetic - behave like a compass. After hatching on beaches around the world they undertake multiyear, epic migrations at sea. The turtles then return to the exact spot where they were born to mate and lay their own eggs.

The story: This is a story about how people can make the difference; people who care and are passionate about these animals. It is not just science. Through a team of dedicated people hundreds of turtles have been saved. In this story we get a close look at these creatures that are now on the list of endangered species and could face extinction.

Existing video footage from rescue, rehab and release of turtles will be used as additional material to visualise the story in a captivating way.

Press Release:


Turtle Rescue
Hundreds of endangered baby turtles wash ashore on the Cape West Coast every year and only a few lucky ones that are rescued and taken to the Two Oceans Aquarium will make it. Carte Blanche meets the aquarium’s team of young marine biologists that has developed a special bond with turtles and nurtures them back to health before releasing them back into the oceans, tracking their movements with the help of satellite tagging.
Producer: Annalise Lubbe
Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


FINAL Script: Turtle Rescue
Date: 10 April 2019
Duration: 8 minutes

V/O It is Tuesday night at the Two Oceans Aquarium in Cape Town. Talitha Noble calls to tell the night staff two baby turtles are about to be dropped off.

Up audio: “The turtles will come in to the front desk, if you can fetch them and then put them in the water…..”

Up natural sound: “Al die pad van Struisbaai”

V/O Noble is the conservation coordinator of the aquarium’s turtle rescue team. It’s teamwork from the start. Tonight’s hatchlings were found on a beach near Struisbaai in the Western Cape and someone from the National Sea Rescue Institute has offered to bring them in.

Up natural sound: “Which tanks Exa? Eleven and twelve.”

Talitha Noble: Two Oceans Aquarium - Conservation coordinator: The animals we get in are really very much at death’s door. They come in, they are at their worst.

Link: This baby loggerhead was found on the shores of Struisbaai last night. He came in here dehydrated, frozen, which shows he has been floating for a long time but right here he has his best chance of survival.

V/O Thousands of baby turtles hatch on the beaches of KwaZulu-Natal every summer. They scramble toward the oceans and swim into the warm Agulhas current flowing south. But some hatchlings drift too close inshore where the Cape’s strong southeastern winds and cold currents take their toll on the cold blooded creatures. Their body temperature drops, their metabolic rate slows down and they go into a state of shock. Too weak to fight they are swept ashore.

Talitha Noble: Two Oceans Aquarium - Conservations Coordinator: They are washed up on the beaches incredibly compromised and they would die if not rescued. So we give them a good little clean, treat their wounds but we try and be quite quick about it, because at this point they are dehydrated and they are cold shocked and they have these injuries so it is getting their body temperature back up to normal. It’s a slow process and requires some time.

V/O From Plettenberg Bay to Muizenberg on the Cape coast, winter is taking its toll. In only five weeks 33 baby turtles have been rescued and brought to the aquarium.

Derek: How do you help them recover?

Talitha Noble: We give them lots of love, primarily good food, healthy nutrition and make sure their environment is clean and sterile and appropriate as possible. Turtles are the most phenomenal animals. They have got this strength and resilience about them and unfortunately they are just incredibly threatened out in the wild.

V/O Noble fell in love with the ocean when she did the Young Biologist course at the Two Oceans Aquarium. For the last few years, she has focused on turtles and works closely with Inge Adams, who shares her passion for these marine creatures.

Inge Adams: Two Oceans Aquarium: Research Coordinator: So it was actually watching National Geographic on a Sunday afternoon with my grandma seeing people like David Attenborough working with animals that inspired this love for the natural world.

Up audio: Inge and Talitha preparing food for the hatchlings

V/O The hatchlings are fed twice a day. Adams records their food intake and other vital data.

Inge Adams: So the moment the turtle arrive, be it a hatchling or larger turtle we record how much it weighs, we measure it to see how big it is and we also record any physical injuries along with other data as to who brought it in and where it was found.

Derek: Data that helps aquariums around the world?

Inge Adams: We have a system called the Zoological Information System or ZIM for short and all aquariums put all their data on the system and what is really great is that all other aquariums around the world can access this system and see what is happening at the two oceans aquarium.

V/O When the Two Oceans Aquarium opened its doors in 1995 staff had no intention of keeping turtles. But then, they received the first call for help.

Maryke Musson: Two Oceans Aquarium - Curator: We got a phone call from a Japanese vessel here in the port of Cape Town and they said they have a little turtle on board with an injury can we come and fetch it, and it was this sweet little 2kg turtle with an injury on its shell and we brought it back and we of course had to learn to look after this turtle.

V/O They named her Yoshi and she became the inspiration behind the turtle project.

Maryke Musson: And through working with her we learnt so much that we started taking in stranded hatchlings or other injured turtles. So since 2009 we have rehabilitated and released about 500 turtles which is incredible because every single one of those turtles would have died if it did not end up here.

Link: The larger turtles are kept here with the rays and the black muscle crackers; along with medical attention and good nutrition they are given a chance to recover to grow strong and be released into the ocean once again.

V/O Turtles have an extremely low survival rate and only one in every thousand hatchlings reach maturity. Sandy, a sub-adult green turtle, was a victim of a boat propeller accident. Dr Brandon Spolander and the team helped her pull through.

Dr. Brandon Spolander: Two Oceans Aquarium - Veterinarian: When she first arrived she had these incredibly deep injuries to the top of the body which had actually penetrated right through into the cavity of the body. So there was a lot of cleaning of the wound and through that whole process you have to maintain her vital functions to help the body repair.

V/O There are only seven turtles species in the world of which three are endangered. Sandy was on that list. Through human actions such as habitat destruction, poaching and plastic pollution we have threatened their survival. Million of tonnes of plastic enter the oceans each year putting their lives at risk.

Link: Leatherback turtles mainly feed on jellyfish. Floating plastic is one of the biggest dangers for these marine animals. They sometimes mistake a plastic bag for food.

V/O But Leatherbacks are not the only ones at risk. Bob and Alvi, also green turtles like Sandy, were both victims of plastic pollution.

Dr. Brandon Spolander: That’s where it is really shocking. Not just your overt big cases of a larger turtle having a blockage like Alvi but where it really, really strikes you you have these baby, baby turtles who have not been in the water very long. We actually see them defecate very small particles of plastic, big enough to see with the naked eye but the fact that they are so young, so small, being in the sea for such a short time frame and already 80% of them are ingesting and excreting plastic.

Up audio: So we have a new little chap here

V/O From hatchlings barely weighing 12 grams, to juveniles with injured flippers and mature turtles, it takes all kind of treatment to heal their injuries.

Link: A lot of fret but we are going to visit Alvi and Bob to see how they are doing in the ocean exhibit.

V/O When Bob and Alvi are ready to be released, they will be fitted with a satellite tagging system that will provide valuable information about their movements. Four years ago, the aquarium started tagging the larger turtles with huge success. Kevin Spiby heads the tracking team.

Derek: How long do these transmitters last for?

Kevin Spiby: Two Oceans Aquarium: Senior Biologist. I depends on the type of data you want to collect; ours will last in the region of between 18 months and two years. Ours transmit every time they surface, it collects data every 15 seconds.

V/O It took Sandy two years to recover from her boat propeller injury. She was released in December last year. Since then, Sandy has covered a distance of more than 12 000 kilometres.

Up audio: “Now she is spending most of her time between Elands Bay and Lamberts Bay on our west coast.”

Talitha Noble: We joke and say she is surfing. Many of these turtles are with us for years and you really form a connection with them and to be carry to pass that on after the release is exciting, the value of the data is immeasurable it is really quite phenomenal.

__________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Sunday promo:
Derek: Every year hundreds of baby turtles are caught up in cold currents, too weak to fight they are washed up dehydrated and half frozen; here they are given a second chance.

Promo 1:
V/O Hundreds of baby turtles get caught up in the cold currents of the Cape and washed ashore. At the Two Oceans Aquarium they get a second chance.
Talitha Noble: The turtles we get in are really very much at death’s door.

Promo 2:
Plastic pollution and cold currents threaten baby turtles that end up on Cape beaches but a team of marine biologist are saving the lives of the lucky few that are brought in for rehabilitation.

Promo 3:
A young team of Two Oceans marine biologist has given hope to injured turtles, nursing them back to health. Once released into the ocean they are able to track their movements with satellite tagging.

Carte Blanche meets the aquarium’s team of young marine biologists that has developed a special bond with turtles and nurtures them back to health before releasing them back into the oceans, tracking their movements with the help of satellite tagging. Producer: Annalise Lubbe Presenter: Derek Watts Script: FINAL Script: Turtle Rescue Date: 10 April 2019 Duration: 8 minutes V/O It is Tuesday night at the Two Oceans Aquarium in Cape Town. Talitha Noble calls to tell the night staff two baby turtles are about to be dropped off. Up audio: “The turtles will come in to the front desk, if you can fetch them and then put them in the water…..” Up natural sound: “Al die pad van Struisbaai” V/O Noble is the conservation coordinator of the aquarium’s turtle rescue team. It’s teamwork from the start. Tonight’s hatchlings were found on a beach near Struisbaai in the Western Cape and someone from the National Sea Rescue Institute has offered to bring them in. Up natural sound: “Which tanks Exa? Eleven and twelve.” Talitha Noble: Two Oceans Aquarium - Conservation coordinator: The animals we get in are really very much at death’s door. They come in, they are at their worst. Link: This baby loggerhead was found on the shores of Struisbaai last night. He came in here dehydrated, frozen, which shows he has been floating for a long time but right here he has his best chance of survival. V/O Thousands of baby turtles hatch on the beaches of KwaZulu-Natal every summer. They scramble toward the oceans and swim into the warm Agulhas current flowing south. But some hatchlings drift too close inshore where the Cape’s strong southeastern winds and cold currents take their toll on the cold blooded creatures. Their body temperature drops, their metabolic rate slows down and they go into a state of shock. Too weak to fight they are swept ashore. Talitha Noble: Two Oceans Aquarium - Conservations Coordinator: They are washed up on the beaches incredibly compromised and they would die if not rescued. So we give them a good little clean, treat their wounds but we try and be quite quick about it, because at this point they are dehydrated and they are cold shocked and they have these injuries so it is getting their body temperature back up to normal. It’s a slow process and requires some time. V/O From Plettenberg Bay to Muizenberg on the Cape coast, winter is taking its toll. In only five weeks 33 baby turtles have been rescued and brought to the aquarium. Derek: How do you help them recover? Talitha Noble: We give them lots of love, primarily good food, healthy nutrition and make sure their environment is clean and sterile and appropriate as possible. Turtles are the most phenomenal animals. They have got this strength and resilience about them and unfortunately they are just incredibly threatened out in the wild. V/O Noble fell in love with the ocean when she did the Young Biologist course at the Two Oceans Aquarium. For the last few years, she has focused on turtles and works closely with Inge Adams, who shares her passion for these marine creatures. Inge Adams: Two Oceans Aquarium: Research Coordinator: So it was actually watching National Geographic on a Sunday afternoon with my grandma seeing people like David Attenborough working with animals that inspired this love for the natural world. Up audio: Inge and Talitha preparing food for the hatchlings V/O The hatchlings are fed twice a day. Adams records their food intake and other vital data. Inge Adams: So the moment the turtle arrive, be it a hatchling or larger turtle we record how much it weighs, we measure it to see how big it is and we also record any physical injuries along with other data as to who brought it in and where it was found. Derek: Data that helps aquariums around the world? Inge Adams: We have a system called the Zoological Information System or ZIM for short and all aquariums put all their data on the system and what is really great is that all other aquariums around the world can access this system and see what is happening at the two oceans aquarium. V/O When the Two Oceans Aquarium opened its doors in 1995 staff had no intention of keeping turtles. But then, they received the first call for help. Maryke Musson: Two Oceans Aquarium - Curator: We got a phone call from a Japanese vessel here in the port of Cape Town and they said they have a little turtle on board with an injury can we come and fetch it, and it was this sweet little 2kg turtle with an injury on its shell and we brought it back and we of course had to learn to look after this turtle. V/O They named her Yoshi and she became the inspiration behind the turtle project. Maryke Musson: And through working with her we learnt so much that we started taking in stranded hatchlings or other injured turtles. So since 2009 we have rehabilitated and released about 500 turtles which is incredible because every single one of those turtles would have died if it did not end up here. Link: The larger turtles are kept here with the rays and the black muscle crackers; along with medical attention and good nutrition they are given a chance to recover to grow strong and be released into the ocean once again. V/O Turtles have an extremely low survival rate and only one in every thousand hatchlings reach maturity. Sandy, a sub-adult green turtle, was a victim of a boat propeller accident. Dr Brandon Spolander and the team helped her pull through. Dr. Brandon Spolander: Two Oceans Aquarium - Veterinarian: When she first arrived she had these incredibly deep injuries to the top of the body which had actually penetrated right through into the cavity of the body. So there was a lot of cleaning of the wound and through that whole process you have to maintain her vital functions to help the body repair. V/O There are only seven turtles species in the world of which three are endangered. Sandy was on that list. Through human actions such as habitat destruction, poaching and plastic pollution we have threatened their survival. Million of tonnes of plastic enter the oceans each year putting their lives at risk. Link: Leatherback turtles mainly feed on jellyfish. Floating plastic is one of the biggest dangers for these marine animals. They sometimes mistake a plastic bag for food. V/O But Leatherbacks are not the only ones at risk. Bob and Alvi, also green turtles like Sandy, were both victims of plastic pollution. Dr. Brandon Spolander: That’s where it is really shocking. Not just your overt big cases of a larger turtle having a blockage like Alvi but where it really, really strikes you you have these baby, baby turtles who have not been in the water very long. We actually see them defecate very small particles of plastic, big enough to see with the naked eye but the fact that they are so young, so small, being in the sea for such a short time frame and already 80% of them are ingesting and excreting plastic. Up audio: So we have a new little chap here V/O From hatchlings barely weighing 12 grams, to juveniles with injured flippers and mature turtles, it takes all kind of treatment to heal their injuries. Link: A lot of fret but we are going to visit Alvi and Bob to see how they are doing in the ocean exhibit. V/O When Bob and Alvi are ready to be released, they will be fitted with a satellite tagging system that will provide valuable information about their movements. Four years ago, the aquarium started tagging the larger turtles with huge success. Kevin Spiby heads the tracking team. Derek: How long do these transmitters last for? Kevin Spiby: Two Oceans Aquarium: Senior Biologist. I depends on the type of data you want to collect; ours will last in the region of between 18 months and two years. Ours transmit every time they surface, it collects data every 15 seconds. V/O It took Sandy two years to recover from her boat propeller injury. She was released in December last year. Since then, Sandy has covered a distance of more than 12 000 kilometres. Up audio: “Now she is spending most of her time between Elands Bay and Lamberts Bay on our west coast.” Talitha Noble: We joke and say she is surfing. Many of these turtles are with us for years and you really form a connection with them and to be carry to pass that on after the release is exciting, the value of the data is immeasurable it is really quite phenomenal. __________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Sunday promo: Derek: Every year hundreds of baby turtles are caught up in cold currents, too weak to fight they are washed up dehydrated and half frozen; here they are given a second chance. Promo 1: V/O Hundreds of baby turtles get caught up in the cold currents of the Cape and washed ashore. At the Two Oceans Aquarium they get a second chance. Talitha Noble: The turtles we get in are really very much at death’s door. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Every year dozens of baby turtles wash out on the beaches of the cape. If not rescued they will die. Carte Blanche investigates.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: From March till September is a busy time for the Two Oceans Aquarium when sea turtles are being brought in to their rehabilitation centre. These tiny sea creatures are found frozen on the beaches of the Cape coast lifeless and still. They are cold and starving, suffering from dehydration and hypothermia and in a permanent state of shock. Referred to as ‘cold stunning’ their heart rate have decreased to a point that they will die if not rescued.
metadata.Summary: Turtles are cold blooded and cannot warm themselves. They thrive in the warm waters of KwaZulu-Natal and Mozambique where they breed during the summer months. They lay their eggs onshore in the the sand and after 60 days these tiny animals fight their way into the sea heading into the warm current where they drift and float whilst feeding. But some get lost in stormy seas and cross currents drifting kilometres south into the icy waters of the cape. From Plettenberg Bay on the east coast to Witsand on the west coast it is believed that hundreds of turtles wash ashore every year but only a few are the lucky ones found by passers by and picked up. Human intervention is needed to rescue the stranded animals; some with injuries and damaged flippers they are in urgent need of medical attention. But it is not only the babies that need rescuing; adult turtles are often found by fisherman or divers out in the open seas where they are entangled in fishing lines. Plastic bags that float in the ocean looks like jellyfish, a staple diet of loggerhead turtles who are often found with plastic in their gut. Even baby turtles poop minute plastic pellets called nurdles that have become one of the biggest polluters of our oceans. From Loggerheads to Leatherbacks, all seven species of turtles found in South Africa has been treated by a team of experts at the Two Oceans rehabilitation centre since its inception in 2009. They have seen the damage first hand that man causes: from treating infected and gashed carapice caused by boat propellers to removing plastic bags from the gut of a Loggerhead, they have managed to turn the statistics around.
metadata.Further information: Talitha Noble, a 28 year old marine biologist working at the Two Oceans Aquarium has developed a special bond with turtles. Her daily job consist of feeding them a special diet, monitoring their growth, exercising the ones with damaged flippers and getting them ready to be released back into the ocean when they are strong enough. She says “they are my babies and have given me life lessons that no other school could have done. They come in here in all shapes and forms, some hardly breathing and when they leave, I have say goodbye to some very special ones like Sandy. Sandy, a Green Turtle, was found near Witsand 2016 with big gashes through her carapace. It was suspected that she was hit by a boat propeller: we cleaned her wounds, removed the sand and debris under her damaged carapace; disinfected her and constantly monitored her progress and two years later we were able to release her. The amazing thing about science is that we are able to track her movements from the satellite tagging system we installed on the top of her carapice. Sandy has spent most of her time moving between Elands Bay and Lambert’s bay. She has now covered 1 223km, at an average pace of about 16 km per day. Kevin Spiby, is the expert on fitting the satellite tracking system onto the adult turtles and making sure the batteries are in place and the system is working 100% before the release. He has been part of the team since inception and has got the fitting of the satellite system to the carapace down to a tee. Monitoring the movements of the turtles is the job of Maryke Mosson, the curator of the aquarium. She tracks their location and where they are heading for; how many kilometres they swim a day and how long they are stationed in each part of the ocean. This valuable data provides a reliable source of information on each of the adult turtles they have released back into the wild. Twenty-six year old Inge Adams got hooked onto wildlife when she was a kid watching National Geographic programmes at her grandmother’s house. Today she is the youngest of the team with a master’s degree in marine biology. “I have found that my biggest strength comes from the fact that I see women as powerful and role models - gone are the days that a science team consisted of males only. Our sea turtles have been ambassadors for us and through their resilience and feistiness we learn life lessons ourselves and have given many children who have never laid their eyes on these creatures the chance to see them up close and learn about them. “My day to day job is to gather data which becomes part of the studies of the turtle which I hope will give us a new insight into their behavioural patterns.” One of my favourites was Noci, a male loggerhead found near Witsand In April 2018 with major external injuries. He had barnacles on his carapace which indicated that he had been floating for some time. Our vet treated him with antifungal creams, vitamins, antibiotics and together we nursed him back to life. Noci and Sandy have both been back in the ocean for 78 days, and Noci, has racked up the fastest average speed of all our tagged turtles. He has covered a very impressive 4122 km since release in December, with an average pace of 53 km per day. In December last year 14 juveniles were released together with Moya, a green turtle found near Sedgefield in October 2017 that had large open wounds on his flipper and totally dehydrated. Pemba, an olive ridley turtle has travelled 14 388 km over the last year and is currently 1 917 km west of Africa. Just another 3 500 km to go and she will be off the coast of Brazil, where many Olive Ridley turtles breed. Yoshi covered more than 18 500 km averaging 39.4 km per day. Since her release Yoshi has crossed various borders, against the currents and right now it appears as if Yoshi is swimming towards Australia where Loggerhead turtles nest. Why are they amazing? Sea turtles have their own internal compass and can therefor adjust the direction in which they swim. They are able to sense the earth's magnetic field. Deep inside their brains, tiny crystals of a mineral called magnetite - which is magnetic - behave like a compass. After hatching on beaches around the world they undertake multiyear, epic migrations at sea. The turtles then return to the exact spot where they were born to mate and lay their own eggs. The story: This is a story about how people can make the difference; people who care and are passionate about these animals. It is not just science. Through a team of dedicated people hundreds of turtles have been saved. In this story we get a close look at these creatures that are now on the list of endangered species and could face extinction. Existing video footage from rescue, rehab and release of turtles will be used as additional material to visualise the story in a captivating way.
